title: On the Challenges of Transforming UVL to IVML
authors: Prankur Agarwal, Kevin Feichtinger, Klaus Schmid, Holger Eichelberger, Rick Rabiser
text:
Software Product Line (SPL) engineering encourages the reuse of predefined software artifacts for creating tailored variations of the same software to meet specific customer requirements [1,2]. Variability modeling plays a crucial role in SPL engineering [1,3] as it allows capturing the common and variable characteristics of a set of (software) systems in dedicated models [4]. These models are then used to derive and customize different software products with varying features and functionalities [4].

Over the past 30 years, various variability modeling approaches have been developed, each having their own advantages and disadvantages [4,5,6,7,8,9]. The Feature-Oriented Domain Analysis (FODA) approach, introduced by [10], is the basis of most feature modeling approaches available today. Another approach is decision modeling, which has been influenced by the Synthesis method [11,12]. Even within a single approach, there are multiple variants. For example, in feature modeling, one can use academic approaches/tools such as FeatureIDE [13] or commercial ones such as pure::variants [14]. Similarly, in decision modeling, one can use DOPLER [15] or Integrated Variability Modeling Language (IVML) [16,17]. Beyond these common approaches [18] also textual variability modeling languages [19], Orthogonal Variability Modeling (OVM) [3], Unified Modeling Language (UML)-based variability modeling [20], and the Common Variability Language (CVL) [21] are available. Additionally, various open-source communities and industries have developed their own solutions to model variability. For instance, the KConfig language supporting configuration of the Linux Kernel [22] and the Component Definition Language (CDL) [23] from the eCos [24] operating system. Despite numerous efforts, such as the CVL [21] or Universal Variability Language (UVL) [25], there is no officially accepted standard in the variability modeling community, today.

The lack of standardization has led to the need for tools that support multiple variability modeling languages through importers and exporters. However, most of these approaches and tools have a limited lifespan [5,26,27,28]. As a result, researchers and practitioners often resort to creating new approaches instead of exploring existing ones [29] and potentially re-using, customizing, and integrating them. However, various differences among approaches make it hard for researchers and practitioners to compare their advantages and disadvantages. Thus, it would be advantageous to concentrate on enhancing the interoperability of current variability modeling tools [28] to choose the most suitable approach for a given use case. TRAVART [30] was developed to increase the interoperability of existing variability modeling tools by transforming different variability models into each other while preserving the variability to its maximum by minimizing information loss [31]. TRAVART [30] uses UVL [25] as a pivot language and already supports various variability modeling languages like FeatureIDE feature models [13], DOPLER [15], OVM [3], Product-Process-Resource Domain-Specific Language (PPR-DSL) [32,33], and pure::variants [14,34]. However, there are many more languages that are currently not supported, such as the IVML [16].

In this paper, we discuss the differences between UVL [25] and IVML [16] and the resulting challenges for their transformation. We also describe the process of deriving and developing transformations from UVL [25] to IVML [16] using TRAVART [30].
